findings.title: CodeWhale: exec_shell parallel-readonly classifier auto-approves fd/rg/git grep exec flags enabling silent RCE
findings.summary:
### Maintainer resolution

The CodeWhale maintainers validated this report. CodeWhale 0.8.67 and earlier are affected. Version 0.9.0 contains the fix in commit 208421b9d23d81cea3311a1eeb2a2ea81d637686. Users should upgrade to 0.9.0 or later. The original reporter analysis is preserved below.

## Summary
The interactive Agent profile of DeepSeek-TUI (CodeWhale) is explicitly documented to gate **every** shell command behind an approval prompt (config.rs:3725-3736). However, `ExecShellTool::approval_requirement_for(&tool_input)` downgrades the requirement from `Required` to `Auto` for any command the classifier deems "parallel read-only" (shell.rs:2314-2320). `registered_tool_approval_required` returns `false` for `Auto` **before** the `auto_approve` check runs (turn_loop.rs:37-38), so no prompt is shown even for a user who never enabled YOLO. The classifier `is_parallel_readonly_command` (command_safety.rs:389) rejects only shell metacharacters and then matches the flag-stripped base command name against an allowlist that includes `fd`, `rg`, and `git grep`. Those tools execute arbitrary external programs through documented flags (`fd -x/--exec`, `rg --pre`, `git grep --open-files-in-pager`) that need **no** shell metacharacters — yielding silent arbitrary-program execution in the default profile. Same silent-RCE class as CVE-2026-45311 (run_tests) but via a different, unpatched tool and code path.

## Root Cause
`approval_requirement_for` downgrades `exec_shell` to `Auto` when `exec_shell_input_is_parallel_readonly` returns true (shell.rs:2314-2320). The classifier strips all flags and matches the base command name against `PARALLEL_READONLY_PREFIXES` (command_safety.rs:363-385, 419-433). `fd`/`rg` are absent from `COMMAND_ARITY`, so `fd -x cp {} /tmp/exfil` canonicalizes to `"fd"` ∈ allowlist. The only remaining gate at the execute sink is `analyze_command`, which rates `fd`/`rg` as `Safe` (SAFE_COMMANDS command_safety.rs:527,530), so the `SafetyLevel::Dangerous`-o

findings.title: CodeWhale: Automation auto_approve defaults to true, bypassing the task-path hardening fix for silent recurring agent execution
findings.summary:
### Maintainer resolution

The CodeWhale maintainers validated this report. CodeWhale 0.8.67 and earlier are affected. Version 0.9.0 contains the fix in commit 208421b9d23d81cea3311a1eeb2a2ea81d637686. Users should upgrade to 0.9.0 or later. The original reporter analysis is preserved below.

## Summary
CVE-2026-45374 (GHSA-72w5-pf8h-xfp4) hardened the task path so auto-approval must be opted into explicitly: `add_task` uses `req.auto_approve.unwrap_or(false)` (task_manager.rs:868). The automation subsystem was not hardened in kind. `AutomationRecord::task_auto_approve()` resolves an omitted `auto_approve` to `DEFAULT_AUTOMATION_AUTO_APPROVE = true` (automation_manager.rs:29, 101-103), and `enqueue_run_task` builds the `NewTaskRequest` with `auto_approve: Some(automation.task_auto_approve())` — i.e. an explicit `Some(true)` (automation_manager.rs:766). Because the field is `Some`, `unwrap_or(false)` returns `true` and the seed-2 default is bypassed. That `true` propagates to `ApprovalMode::Bypass` (runtime_threads.rs:2253), where the background approval loop auto-approves every tool call with no human present (runtime_threads.rs:3383-3416). One approved `automation_create` becomes a durable, recurring, fully auto-approved agent. Same insecure-default class as CVE-2026-45374, on a different, unpatched subsystem.

## Root Cause
Sibling durable defaults in the same struct are safe — `DEFAULT_AUTOMATION_ALLOW_SHELL = false` and `DEFAULT_AUTOMATION_TRUST_MODE = false` (automation_manager.rs:27-28) — while `DEFAULT_AUTOMATION_AUTO_APPROVE` alone defaults `true` (:29). `create_automation` stores `auto_approve: None` when omitted (:422); `task_auto_approve()` resolves `None`→`true` (:101-103); `enqueue_run_task` passes `Some(true)` (:766), defeating `add_task`'s `unwrap_or(false)` seed fix. The `automation_create` tool schema also declares `"auto_approve": {"type":"boolean","default":true}` (tools/automation.rs:49) while sibling `allow_shell`/`trust_mode` default `false`.

findings.title: mssql-mcp-core: SQL injection in mssql-mcp write tools via unparameterized table names and WHERE clauses
findings.summary:
Several tools in `mssql-mcp-core` built T-SQL by string-interpolating caller-supplied identifiers and predicates directly into the statement passed to the node-mssql `Request.query()` batch API. Only data values were parameterized.

Affected tools and inputs:
- `update_data`, `delete_data`: `tableName` and the free-form `whereClause` were interpolated raw.
- `insert_data`: `tableName` and column names (object keys) were interpolated raw.
- `execute_transaction`: the same raw `tableName`/`whereClause` interpolation per operation.
- `create_table`, `create_index`, `drop_table`: table/column/index/schema identifiers were interpolated with no or insufficient validation.
- `list_databases` (reader tier): the `stateFilter` argument was interpolated raw into the query, with only a non-enforced inputSchema enum guarding it.

The only check on `whereClause` was that it was non-empty. Because the row-count and preview queries run before the `confirmUpdate`/`confirmDelete` step, a malicious `whereClause` or `tableName` executed on the first call, bypassing the preview/confirmation and `maxRows` safety controls. `Request.query()` submits a multi-statement T-SQL batch, so a crafted input enabled stacked statements (arbitrary DDL/DML), sub-selects, and (with a privileged login and `xp_cmdshell` enabled) OS command execution. Because `list_databases` is a read-only tool, the `stateFilter` sink makes the reader package injectable as well.

## Impact

An actor who can supply tool arguments (a malicious or compromised MCP client, or an LLM agent steered via indirect prompt injection) could read, modify, or drop arbitrary data, bypass the `read_data` allow/deny validation and the preview/confirmation/`maxRows` safeguards, and conditionally achieve OS command execution.

## Patches

Fixed in `@connorbritain/mssql-mcp-core` 0.6.0:
- All identifiers are validated against a strict allowlist and bracket-quoted via a shared helper.
- The free-form `whereClause` string parameter is removed (

findings.title: NLTK: ARFF_Formatter Injects Weka ARFF Schema Directives via Attacker-Controlled Class Labels
findings.summary:
## Description

### Summary

`nltk.classify.weka.ARFF_Formatter` writes class labels directly into the Weka ARFF `@ATTRIBUTE '-label-' {...}` declaration without any ARFF quoting or escaping. An attacker who can contribute class labels to a training dataset can include ARFF metacharacters such as `}`, newlines, `@ATTRIBUTE`, and `@DATA` to break out of the nominal label list and inject attacker‑controlled ARFF schema and data directives.

This vulnerability is reachable in any application that calls `WekaClassifier.train()` or `ARFF_Formatter.from_train()` with attacker‑influenced training data. The victim does not need to manually edit the ARFF file; the normal training workflow writes the malformed ARFF automatically.

### Technical Details

The vulnerable code path is:

1. `WekaClassifier.train()` calls `ARFF_Formatter.from_train(featuresets)`.
2. `from_train()` extracts labels from the training data and passes them to `ARFF_Formatter(labels, features)`.
3. `header_section()` uses `",".join(self._labels)` directly, embedding attacker‑controlled strings into the ARFF header without sanitization.

Because the label names are not escaped, a label containing `safe}\n@ATTRIBUTE injected NUMERIC\n@DATA\n0,owned\n%` will close the label set, inject a new attribute, start a premature data section, and comment out the remaining header.

### Proof of Concept

The following self‑contained Python script demonstrates the vulnerability. It requires only NLTK and does **not** need Weka to be installed, because the attack is carried out purely by generating the ARFF string.

```python
from nltk.classify.weka import ARFF_Formatter

# Attacker‑controlled label containing ARFF metacharacters.
# The `}` closes the label set, the `@ATTRIBUTE` injects a new attribute,
# `@DATA` starts the data section early, and `%` comments out the rest.
malicious_label = "safe}\n@ATTRIBUTE injected NUMERIC\n@DATA\n0,owned\n%"

featuresets = [
    ({"f": "benign"}, "legit"),          # legitimate exa

findings.title: NLTK: Uncontrolled recursion in DependencyGraph traversal causes denial of service via deep dependency chains
findings.summary:
## Root Cause
The dependency-graph traversal helpers recurse over dependency links without any depth
bound or visited set. `DependencyGraph._tree` (`nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:404`)
recurses once per dependency link, `triples` (`nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:432`) is a
recursive generator, and `get_cycle_path` (`nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:520`) recurses
over dependencies. The neighbouring `contains_cycle` method was deliberately rewritten as
an iterative depth-first search, but these sibling helpers on the public traversal path
were left recursive with no depth counter.

## Impact
An application that parses an untrusted CoNLL/Malt-TAB dependency structure and then walks
it via `tree()` or `triples()` aborts with an unhandled `RecursionError`, terminating the
affected operation or request worker (denial of service, CWE-674). The recursion is pure
Python, so the result is a catchable `RecursionError`, not memory corruption or code
execution. Confidentiality and integrity are unaffected. `get_cycle_path` additionally
lacks a visited set and will not terminate on a genuine cycle.

## Attack Chain
1. The application constructs `DependencyGraph(conll_str)` from attacker-supplied text
   where token *k*'s head is token *k+1*, forming a linear dependency chain of length *N*.
   Graph construction (`_parse`) is iterative and completes without error.
2. The application calls the public `DependencyGraph.tree()`
   (`nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:408`), which invokes `_tree(root)`.
3. `_tree` recurses once per chain link with no depth guard and no visited set, consuming
   one stack frame per link (the list comprehension costs roughly two frames per level).
4. Once the chain length exceeds the interpreter recursion limit, an unhandled
   `RecursionError` propagates out of the public API. `triples()` fails the same way.

## Bypass Evidence
Against the shipped source at the default recursion limit, a chain of length 5 walks
cleanly through `tree()`, while a chain of length

findings.title: NLTK: Uncontrolled recursion in semantic-logic type parser causes denial of service via nested type strings
findings.summary:
## Root Cause
The semantic-logic type parser `read_type` (`nltk/sem/logic.py:866`) recurses on both
halves of every `<a,b>` complex type (`nltk/sem/logic.py:882-884`) with no depth or length
bound — only an `isinstance` assertion and a parenthesis-balance assertion. The
`LogicParser.MAX_PARSE_DEPTH` guard (`nltk/sem/logic.py:107,294`) protects the expression
parser but never runs on the `read_type` path, which is reached directly by the public
`Type.fromstring` classmethod and by signature-string type checking.

## Impact
An application that parses an untrusted type string, or type-checks an expression against
an attacker-influenced signature, aborts with an unhandled `RecursionError`, terminating
the affected operation or request worker (denial of service, CWE-674). The recursion is
pure Python, yielding a catchable `RecursionError` rather than memory corruption or code
execution. Confidentiality and integrity are unaffected. Exposure is narrower than a
general-purpose parser because the input must reach a type-string or signature parameter.

## Attack Chain
1. The application calls `nltk.sem.logic.Type.fromstring(s)` (`nltk/sem/logic.py:736`) — or
   `Expression.typecheck(signature)` / `Expression.fromstring(expr, type_check=True,
   signature=...)`, which reach `read_type` for each type-string signature value
   (`nltk/sem/logic.py:1080`) — with a deeply nested type string such as
   `"<" * n + "e,e" + ">" * n`.
2. `Type.fromstring` passes the string straight to `read_type` with no length or depth
   check (only assertions on type and parenthesis balance).
3. `read_type` recurses on both halves of each `<a,b>` level, consuming one stack frame per
   nesting level; the `MAX_PARSE_DEPTH` guard on the separate `LogicParser` class does not
   execute here.
4. Once the depth exceeds the interpreter recursion limit, an unhandled `RecursionError`
   propagates out of the public API.

findings.title: NLTK: Uncontrolled recursion in Tree.fromlist causes denial of service via deeply nested list input
findings.summary:
## Root Cause
`Tree.fromlist` (`nltk/tree/tree.py:767`) converts a nested list into a `Tree` by recursing
once per nesting level (`nltk/tree/tree.py:780`) with no depth bound — its only validation
is `type(l) == list and len(l) > 0`. The sibling constructor `Tree.fromstring` was hardened
with a `MAX_TREE_DEPTH` cap (`nltk/tree/tree.py:31,695`) that rejects adversarially deep
input with a bounded `ValueError`, but that guard was not applied to `fromlist`, which
builds `Tree` objects identically.

## Impact
An application that builds a `Tree` from an attacker-controlled nested list — for example
`Tree.fromlist(json.loads(untrusted))` — aborts with an unhandled `RecursionError`,
terminating the affected operation or request worker (denial of service, CWE-674). Any
later recursive traversal of an over-deep tree (`height`, `pformat`, equality) fails the
same way. The recursion is pure Python, yielding a catchable `RecursionError` rather than
memory corruption or code execution. Confidentiality and integrity are unaffected.

## Attack Chain
1. The application obtains an attacker-controlled deeply nested list, typically by decoding
   an untrusted JSON payload, and calls `nltk.tree.Tree.fromlist(l)`.
2. `fromlist` checks only that the argument is a non-empty list; it applies no depth cap.
3. `fromlist` recurses once per nesting level, consuming call-stack frames; the
   `MAX_TREE_DEPTH` guard used by `fromstring` is never invoked on this path.
4. Once the nesting depth exceeds the interpreter recursion limit, an unhandled
   `RecursionError` propagates out of the public API.

findings.title: NLTK: Uncontrolled recursion in Toolbox settings helpers causes denial of service via deeply nested input
findings.summary:
## Root Cause
The Toolbox settings-tree helpers recurse over the parsed element tree without any depth
bound. `_to_settings_string` (`nltk/toolbox.py:418`), `remove_blanks`
(`nltk/toolbox.py:432`), `add_default_fields` (`nltk/toolbox.py:451`), `_sort_fields`
(`nltk/toolbox.py:484`), and `add_blank_lines` (`nltk/toolbox.py:502,516`) each recurse once
per element level with no depth counter or explicit stack. The producer
`ToolboxSettings.parse` builds the element tree iteratively, so nesting depth is driven
entirely by attacker-supplied `\+marker` / `\-marker` pairs.

An application that parses an untrusted Toolbox settings file and then serialises or
transforms it through any of the public helper functions aborts with an unhandled
`RecursionError`, terminating the affected operation or request worker (denial of service,
CWE-674). The recursion is pure Python, yielding a catchable `RecursionError` rather than
memory corruption or code execution. Confidentiality and integrity are unaffected.

findings.title: NLTK: Uncontrolled recursion in WordNet Synset hypernym walkers (max_depth/min_depth/hypernym_paths/hypernym_distances) causes DoS
findings.summary:
## Summary

Four hypernym-walking methods on the WordNet `Synset` class in `nltk/corpus/reader/wordnet.py` (`max_depth`, `min_depth`, `hypernym_paths`, and `hypernym_distances`) traverse the hypernym pointer graph by direct recursion with no visited-node set and no depth cap. WordNet `data.<pos>` file content is untrusted corpus input in NLTK, the same trust boundary the project already treats as attacker-controlled across its corpus-content hardening work. When the parsed hypernym graph contains a cycle, or a chain deeper than the interpreter recursion limit, these methods recurse without bound and raise an uncaught `RecursionError`, aborting the traversal and any worker that does not catch it. No special privileges are needed; the victim only has to load an attacker-supplied corpus and call any of several shipped public methods that reach these walkers.

## Root Cause

`Synset.max_depth` computes `1 + max(h.max_depth() for h in hypernyms)` and only assigns its `_max_depth` memo after that recursive expression fully returns. Because Python evaluates the right-hand side completely before binding the left-hand side, the memo is never set on a node that is still on the recursion stack, so a cyclic graph re-enters the same not-yet-memoized node indefinitely. `min_depth`, `hypernym_paths`, and `hypernym_distances` follow the same recursive descent with no cycle detection. The security invariant that graph traversal over untrusted corpus data must terminate is violated: the pointer offsets parsed from the data file are stored verbatim with no graph-shape validation, so the attacker controls the graph topology. The sibling walkers in the same class (`closure`, `tree`, `_shortest_hypernym_paths`) were hardened with acyclic/visited guards, which shows cyclic hypernym graphs are an in-scope threat that these four methods simply were not converted to handle.

  Synset.max_depth          (nltk/corpus/reader/wordnet.p

findings.title: NLTK: StreamBackedCorpusView constructor os.stat leaks out-of-root file existence, size, and mtime bypassing pathsec ENFORCE
findings.summary:
## Summary

`StreamBackedCorpusView`, a public API in `nltk/corpus/reader/util.py`, applies the pathsec sandbox to the file content it reads but not to the file metadata it probes in its constructor. When the view is created with a plain string fileid, `__init__` calls `os.stat(self._fileid).st_size` with no pathsec validation, so an application that passes an attacker influenced path to the constructor discloses whether an arbitrary out of root file exists and, if it does, its exact byte size and modification time, even when `nltk.pathsec.ENFORCE` is `True`. This is the residual metadata channel left open by the fix for CVE-2026-63312 (GHSA-x5ph-mj9p-rfr8), which closed arbitrary content read on the same code path but did not bring the sibling `os.stat` under the sandbox.

## Root Cause

The pathsec sandbox is intended to confine all NLTK filesystem access to allowed data roots. The fix for CVE-2026-63312 enforced this for content reads by routing `StreamBackedCorpusView._open` through `nltk.pathsec.open` (`_secure_open`). The constructor, however, computes the end of file position eagerly, and on the non `PathPointer` branch it stats the caller supplied path directly. The `PathPointer` branch is validated (it calls `PathPointer.file_size()`), but the plain string branch reaches `os.stat` with no `validate_path`, `_secure_open`, or `required_root` check. The security invariant "no filesystem access outside allowed roots under ENFORCE" is therefore violated for the metadata channel: `os.stat` is filesystem access, and it is performed on the same untrusted string entry point that the content read fix protected.

```text
Affected component: nltk.corpus.reader.util.StreamBackedCorpusView.__init__
Sink:   nltk/corpus/reader/util.py, os.stat(self._fileid).st_size on the plain-string branch
Guarded sibling: _open() (routes through nltk.pathsec.open); the constructor os.stat is not guarded
```

## Impact

An attacker who can influence the fileid string passed to `StreamBac

findings.title: NLTK: Untrusted search path in prover9/mace4 config allows local code execution via relative binary_location
findings.summary:
## Summary
`Prover9Parent.config_prover9(binary_location=...)` (and `Mace`, which inherits it) accepts a relative `binary_location` and passes it as `path_to_bin` to `find_binary`, which disables the CWD-relative rejection guard. Unlike the boxer/senna/malt/repp siblings, prover9/mace apply no `os.path.isabs()` filter, so the resolved relative program path (e.g. `./prover9`) is executed from the current working directory via `subprocess.Popen`. A local attacker who can plant `./prover9` (or `./mace4`) in the resolved directory achieves local code execution.

## Root Cause
`nltk/inference/prover9.py:121-135` calls `find_binary(name, path_to_bin=binary_location, env_vars=["PROVER9"], ...)`. A truthy `path_to_bin` sets `searching_bare_name = not path_to_bin and ...` → False (`internals.py:935`), so the guard `if searching_bare_name and not os.path.isabs(path): continue` (`internals.py:940`) never runs. The result is stored in `self._prover9_bin`; on the next `prove()`, `_call` → `subprocess.Popen([binary]+args, ...)` (`prover9.py:207`) execs it. `Mace(Prover9Parent)` inherits `config_prover9` (`mace.py:229`). findings.title: k8s-mcp-server: Missing authentication on default SSE/HTTP transport allows unauthenticated Kubernetes tool execution
findings.summary:
## Summary
When k8s-mcp-server runs in its default SSE transport mode, the MCP `tools/call`
endpoint is dispatched with no authentication, session token, or Origin check.
Any client that can reach the listening port can enumerate and invoke the
server's Kubernetes tools (including destructive/write tools) without credentials,
executing with the server's configured cluster privileges.

## Affected
Commit be87a6dd72bb6ec1d4886b8548843b99a4638b12 (Merge PR #130)
MCP library: github.com/mark3labs/mcp-go v0.57.0
Default mode: sse (SERVER_MODE default), default port 8080, bind 0.0.0.0

## Root cause (static trace: handleSSE -> handleMessage -> tools/call)
- main.go L129: `server.NewSSEServer(s)` is created with no auth option and no
  contextFunc; L130 `sse.Start(":"+port)` binds all interfaces (0.0.0.0).
- mcp-go sse.go handleSSE (GET /sse): no auth header check; the server mints a
  sessionId for any caller. The sessionId is a correlation value, not a credential.
- handleMessage (POST /message): the only gates are method==POST and a loadable
  sessionId. No Authorization/Bearer/token/Origin/CSRF check before
  `s.server.HandleMessage(ctx, rawMessage)` dispatches to the tools/call handler.
- Only `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` is present (CORS relaxation, not auth).

are all registered unless `-read-only` is set (default readOnly=false).

KUBERNETES_SERVER=https://127.0.0.1:1 (no real cluster touched).

findings.title: containerd image-triggered daemon crash via malformed digest in subject-annotated descriptor
findings.summary:
### Impact

A bug in containerd's image manifest processing causes an unrecovered panic when a child descriptor contains the `io.containerd.manifest.subject` annotation and a malformed digest. Pulling or importing such an image through the transfer service (including default CRI `PullImage` requests) crashes the containerd daemon. In Kubernetes environments, `kubelet` retries failed image pulls with backoff, allowing a pod referencing an untrusted image to repeatedly crash containerd and disrupt container operations on the worker node.

### Patches

This bug has been fixed in containerd 2.4.2, 2.3.7, and 2.2.10. Users should update to these versions to resolve the issue.

### Workarounds

Restrict pod image references to trusted registries (for example, using a Kubernetes `ValidatingAdmissionPolicy` or admission webhook) and only pull or import images from trusted sources.

### Credits

The containerd project would like to thank @melihgurlek, LEI WANG (@ssst0n3) and Haoyuan Zhang (@zj1ng7), and OpenSec Intelligence who independently discovered and responsibly disclosed this issue in accordance with the [containerd security policy](https://github.com/containerd/project/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

### For more information

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory:

* Open an issue in [containerd](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/issues/new/choose)
* Email us at [security@containerd.io](mailto:security@containerd.io)

findings.title: Model Context Protocol Python SDK: OAuth client could send credentials to an authorization server chosen by the MCP server
findings.summary:
### Summary
In affected versions, the SDK's OAuth client support (`mcp.client.auth`) let the MCP server a client connected to decide where the client's OAuth credentials were sent:

- the authorization server metadata `issuer` was not validated on every discovery path, and
- stored or pre-provisioned client credentials were not bound to the authorization server they belong to.

A malicious or compromised MCP server could therefore direct them to a token endpoint of its choosing:

- by naming its own authorization server in its protected resource metadata, or
- by publishing none and serving metadata that presents the user's real authorization server as the `issuer`.

It would then receive the `client_secret`, authorization code and PKCE `code_verifier` meant for that real server (or, with `PrivateKeyJWTOAuthProvider`, a signed client assertion).

### Am I affected?
Yes, if both of these hold:

- your application uses the SDK as an MCP client over HTTP with `OAuthClientProvider`, `ClientCredentialsOAuthProvider`, `PrivateKeyJWTOAuthProvider` or the deprecated 1.x `RFC7523OAuthClientProvider` as the transport's `auth` handler;
- it may connect to an MCP server you do not fully trust while holding credentials for a legitimate authorization server (a pre-provisioned secret or signing key, or a stored client registration).

Affected versions:

- 1.9.1 through 1.29.1: no `issuer` check and no credential binding on any path.
- 2.0.0 through 2.1.1: both missing whenever the server publishes no protected resource metadata (the legacy fallback) or answers `403 insufficient_scope`.
- Both lines, on every path: `ClientCredentialsOAuthProvider` and `PrivateKeyJWTOAuthProvider` had no way to name the authorization server their credentials belong to.

Not affected:

- MCP servers built with the SDK
- stdio clients
- clients that attach their own tokens or headers

findings.title: Mistune: Quadratic-time DoS in parse_link_href via unbounded parenthesis scan on empty-label links
findings.summary:
## Resolution

**Fixed in Mistune 3.3.4.** Upgrade to 3.3.4 or later.

- Affected versions: `< 3.3.4`
- First patched version: `3.3.4`
- Fix: https://github.com/lepture/mistune/compare/v3.3.3...v3.3.4

The reported payload was reproduced against the 3.3.3 release tag and verified to scale approximately linearly against the 3.3.4 release tag.

## Original report

The following report describes the issue before the fix.

## Summary
`parse_link_href` in mistune performs an unbounded parenthesis-balancing scan that runs to end-of-document on each unmatched `(`. Because the empty label `[]` bypasses the `no_close_bracket_before` high-water-mark guard, a single small document of the form `"[](" * N` causes O(N) openers to each drive an O(N) scan, producing O(N²) CPU on the **default** `mistune.html()` renderer with no plugins.

## Root Cause
`parse_link` matches the empty label `[]` (`parse_link_label("[](",1)` returns `('', 2)`), so it reaches the `(` branch and calls `parse_link_href`. That function's scan loop (helpers.py:143-159) advances past characters and increments `level` on each `(`, never finding an unescaped `)` at `level==0`, so it runs to EOF and returns `None`. The cursor then advances only ~2 chars to the next `[](`. The `no_close_bracket_before` high-water mark that keeps the balanced-bracket link path linear is never entered because the empty label matches before that branch; `_mark_no_link_before` only advances past the 2-char label, not the href region.

## Impact
A single unauthenticated request rendering untrusted markdown pins a worker at 100% CPU for tens of seconds. Measured on default `mistune.html`, no plugins: 6KB->0.80s, 12KB->3.15s, 24KB->12.5s, 48KB->49.8s (2x input -> ~3.9x time, clean O(n²)). This is the most severe of the mistune quadratic-DoS findings.

## Proof of Concept
```python
import mistune
md = mistune.create_markdown()   # default HTML renderer, no plugins
md("[](" * 16000)                # ~48KB input stalls a worker ~50s
```

findings.title: Mistune: Quadratic-time DoS in inline image parsing (precedence_scan) bypasses not-is-image guards
findings.summary:
## Resolution

**Fixed in Mistune 3.3.4.** Upgrade to 3.3.4 or later.

- Affected versions: `< 3.3.4`
- First patched version: `3.3.4`
- Fix: https://github.com/lepture/mistune/compare/v3.3.3...v3.3.4

The reported payload was reproduced against the 3.3.3 release tag and verified to scale approximately linearly against the 3.3.4 release tag.

## Original report

The following report describes the issue before the fix.

## Summary
mistune's inline image parsing reaches `precedence_scan` for `![` openers because the two guards that keep the link path linear are both gated behind `not is_image`. A small default-renderer document of the form `"![" * N + "x" + "]" * N` produces O(N²) CPU with no plugins.

## Root Cause
For `![` openers, `is_image` is True, so both linearizing guards are skipped: `if not is_image and pos <= state.no_link_before` (inline_parser.py:141) and `has_nested_link = not is_image and _label_contains_link(...)` (:171). Execution reaches `precedence_scan` (:179) which runs `sc.search(state.src, mark_pos, end_pos)` over the whole image body — O(n) per outer opener, x O(n) openers -> O(n²). `max_image_depth` never fires because the failing scans never produce an image token (`image_depth` stays 0).

## Impact
A single unauthenticated request pins a worker at 100% CPU. Measured on default `mistune.html`, no plugins: 6KB->0.28s, 12KB->1.07s, 24KB->4.20s, 48KB->15.8s (2x input -> ~3.8x time).

## Proof of Concept
```python
import mistune
md = mistune.create_markdown()   # default, no plugins
md("![" * 16000 + "x" + "]" * 16000)
```

## Attack Chain
1. Entry: rendered markdown -> `"!["*N + "x" + "]"*N` (no plugins). Guard: none on input size. Bypass proof: no global cap.
2. Check: `not is_image` guards at inline_parser.py:141 (`no_link_before`) and :171 (`_label_contains_link`). Guard: high-water mark + nested-link short-circuit. Bypass proof: `is_image` is True for `![`, so BOTH guards are gated out; `max_image_depth` (:checked after) measured flat across

findings.title: fzf: Predictable FIFO path in zsh completion allows local symlink attack / arbitrary file overwrite as the victim user (_fzf_feed_fifo)
findings.summary:
### Summary

`shell/completion.zsh` feeds every trigger-driven zsh completion through a FIFO at a predictable, PID-based path in shared `/tmp` (`fzf-complete-fifo-$$`), without checking the failure of `rm -f`/`mkfifo`. On a multi-user host, another local user can pre-create that path as a symlink to a victim-writable file (e.g. `~/.bashrc`), causing the victim's own completion to overwrite it with the completion stream — with attacker-influenced content (e.g. via process names in `ps` output), escalating to code execution at the victim's next login. A pre-created plain FIFO instead leaks/blocks on the completion stream.

### Reporter / Credits:
Sai Sreewathsa Kovalluri, Shon Babu and Kannan K (Researchers), Innspark Solutions https://innspark.in/

### Details

`shell/completion.zsh` (tag 0.74.4, commit a140afeb):

- line ~246: `fifo="${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/fzf-complete-fifo-$$"` — predictable name; shell PIDs are low/guessable and a wide range can be pre-created.
- lines 216-220, verbatim:

```zsh
_fzf_feed_fifo() {
  command rm -f "$1"     # fails (EPERM) on an attacker-owned entry in sticky /tmp — error ignored
  mkfifo "$1"            # fails (EEXIST) — exit status unchecked
  cat <&0 > "$1" &|      # follows the attacker symlink / blocks on the attacker FIFO
}
```

Attack modes (no race required):

1. **File clobber → code execution:** `> "$1"` follows a pre-created symlink, truncating/overwriting a victim-writable file with the completion input stream using the victim's privileges. For kill-completion the stream includes attacker-influenced process names, so planted lines can land in the victim's startup file.
2. **Information leak / hang:** a pre-created plain FIFO makes the victim's `cat` block until the attacker reads the stream (full `ps` output, host lists, variable names).

### PoC

Mechanism verified with the function extracted byte-for-byte from `shell/completion.zsh` (only `&|` → `&`, a syntax port irrelevant to the flaw), reproducing the cross-user `/tmp` pr

findings.summary: Next.js App Router applications that pass binary arguments (such as Uint8Array or Blob values) to functions using the `use cache` directive can produce identical cache keys for distinct arguments, allowing cached results to be shared across users — cross-user disclosure of cached data or cache poisoning. findings.title: Next.js: Cache poisoning of shared fallback shells in Cache Components via request-supplied placeholder route params
findings.summary:
Self-hosted Next.js applications served with `next start` and built with `cacheComponents: true` but without Partial Prefetching accept a request-supplied route param value as a prerender placeholder. One unauthenticated GET request can poison the fallback shell cache entry that a family of routes shares.

Such a route is served from a shell that keeps its never-prerenderable params as placeholders, so every value of those params shares one cache entry. A path segment equal to the percent-encoded, bracketed name of its own route param is treated as an unresolved placeholder, and only that param is deferred. A layout above it then renders its concrete value into the shell during the blocking render, and the result, including its HTTP status, is stored under the shared key.

Depending on the application, the stored entry is one of the following:

- A persistent 404, when the layout rejects the value with `notFound()`: served to every URL under the shell key with `"revalidate": false`, across server restarts, with no error logged.
- A substituted param value, when the layout renders the value: the server-rendered HTML renders the attacker's value for that param in place of the visitor's own. A JavaScript client corrects it on hydration. No markup or script injection is possible, and no data is disclosed.

### Preconditions

1. `cacheComponents: true` with `partialPrefetching` unset or `false`.
2. Self-hosted serving with `next start`.
3. A dynamic route with a prerenderable param (`generateStaticParams`) whose requested value was not generated at build time.
4. At least two never-prerenderable params below it: a layout reading the shallower one inside a Suspense boundary, and a deeper one the request supplies as the placeholder.
5. A blocking fallback shell.

### Workarounds

Set `partialPrefetching: true` in `next.config`. Otherwise, apps should upgrade to the patched version as soon as possible.

findings.title: Effect: ReDoS in Schema.TemplateLiteral compiled regex
findings.summary:
### Impact

`Schema.TemplateLiteral` compiles each `Schema.String` span to the lazy wildcard `[\s\S]*?` and decodes input by running the resulting regular expression against it. When a template has two or more `Schema.String` spans, for example:

```ts
Schema.TemplateLiteral(Schema.String, ":", Schema.String, ":", Schema.String, "X")
```

the regex contains several ambiguous wildcards. A non-matching input makes the backtracking engine try combinations across all of them, so matching time grows cubically with input length. A 5,000-character string of `:` characters blocks the event loop for about 15 seconds.

Applications that decode untrusted input with such a schema are affected. That includes `Schema.decodeUnknown`, `Schema.decodeUnknownSync` and `Schema.is`, and anything built on them, such as `HttpApi` request payloads and `@effect/rpc` payloads.

### Patches

Fixed in `effect@3.22.1` (#6761). Template literals whose spans are all `Schema.String` are now matched with a linear left-to-right scan instead of a regular expression.

### Workarounds

If you can't upgrade, check the input length before the template literal runs. Adding `Schema.maxLength` with `.pipe` doesn't help, because the filter runs after the regex. Put the length check on the input side instead:

```ts
Schema.compose(Schema.String.pipe(Schema.maxLength(256)), MyTemplateLiteral)
```

Rejecting oversized request bodies before they reach the schema also works.

findings.title: iSponsorBlockTV: SSRF via Malicious SSDP Response Spoofing in Local Device Discovery

### Summary
iSponsorBlockTV discovers local smart TV devices via SSDP (Simple Service Discovery Protocol). The `LOCATION` URL from SSDP responses is used to fetch device capabilities without URL validation. findings.title: gosaml2: Unauthenticated panic decrypting an EncryptedAssertion with a short or empty CipherValue
findings.summary:
### Summary

An attacker who can supply a crafted SAML Response for parsing can crash a `gosaml2` service provider by sending an `EncryptedAssertion` with AES-GCM encryption metadata and a `CipherValue` shorter than the GCM nonce size (12 bytes). This is a **distinct issue from [GHSA-hwqm-qvj9-4jr2](https://github.com/russellhaering/gosaml2/security/advisories/GHSA-hwqm-qvj9-4jr2)**, which addressed panics in the AES-CBC decryption path (commit [`3418f9ae09063ff8df0ce1bd93f24e538e614def`](https://github.com/russellhaering/gosaml2/commit/3418f9ae09063ff8df0ce1bd93f24e538e614def), included in `v0.10.0`). That fix added a block-size check for CBC but left the AES-GCM path completely unprotected.

`ValidateEncodedResponse()` decrypts `EncryptedAssertion` nodes before signature or content validation completes. There are two call sites:

1. **Signed Response branch** -- [`decode_response.go#L341`](https://github.com/russellhaering/gosaml2/blob/636e7dda202a4d669644e72404a82616ffcbe004/decode_response.go#L341)

Inside `DecryptBytes()` ([`types/encrypted_assertion.go#L34-L92`](https://github.com/russellhaering/gosaml2/blob/636e7dda202a4d669644e72404a82616ffcbe004/types/encrypted_assertion.go#L34-L92)), the AES-GCM branch ([line 53, `case MethodAES128GCM, MethodAES192GCM, MethodAES256GCM:`](https://github.com/russellhaering/gosaml2/b

findings.title: October: Media Library Crop Handler Bypasses Upload Extension Allowlist
findings.summary:
The Media Library upload handler validates the destination filename against an extension allowlist (`default_extensions`), rejecting types such as `php`, `phtml`, `html`, and `htm`. The image crop handler (`MediaManager::onCropImage` / `cropImage`) did not perform this check. The destination filename was taken from user input, the extension was extracted from it, and the staged bytes were written to the public media folder under that attacker-chosen extension. Combined with the fact that upload accepts any file contents under an allowlisted extension (a PHP payload disguised as `.jpg`), and that the zero-dimension crop branch performs a byte-for-byte `File::copy` rather than re-encoding the pixels, an authenticated backend user with the `media.library.create` permission could write a file with arbitrary extension and arbitrary contents into the public media folder.

**Scope of impact depends on web server configuration.** On a default October CMS install (using the shipped Apache `.htaccess` or `nginx.conf`), PHP execution from the media folder is blocked, so the realistic outcome is stored XSS via `.html` or `.svg` files served from the application origin. On a server that is configured to execute PHP inside the media directory (a non-default but real-world misconfiguration), the same bug becomes remote code execution.

### Impact
- Bypass of the Media Library extension allowlist that the upload path enforces
- Stored XSS on default installs: attacker can write `.html` or `.svg` files served from the application origin, executing script in the browser of any backend user or visitor who opens the file
- SVG sanitizer bypass: the `Html::cleanVector` step only runs on the upload path, so uploading malicious SVG content as a `.jpg` and then cropping it to `.svg` skips the sanitizer entirely
- Remote code execution on deployments that execute PHP inside the media folder (non-default)
- Requires authenticated backend access with the `media.library.create` permission

Gortex: Arbitrary file write / repo-confinement escape in `write_file` / `edit_file` / `move_inline` MCP tools → code execution
findings.summary:
### Summary
Gortex is an MCP server exposing `write_file`, `edit_file`, and `move_inline` tools. `resolveFilePath` **exempts absolute paths** from confinement, and the write handlers — unlike `read_file` / `get_symbol_source` — **never call `guardSymlinkWithinRepo`**. A single MCP `write_file` call with an absolute path writes any file the daemon user can, **outside every indexed repo root** (`AtomicWriteFile`'s `MkdirAll` auto-creates missing parents). Writing `~/.zshrc`, `~/.bashrc`, `.git/hooks/pre-commit`, or a cron/systemd unit yields code execution on the next shell/commit. This directly violates the project's own `SECURITY.md` invariant *"File-path resolution is **confined to indexed repository roots**"*

### Affected
`internal/mcp/tools_fileops.go` (+ `tools_move_inline.go`), HEAD `28fa017` (v0.53.0).
**CWE-22** (Path Traversal) / **CWE-73** (External Control of File Name/Path) → **CWE-94** (code execution).

### Vulnerable code
`internal/mcp/tools_fileops.go:54-62` `resolveFilePath` exempts absolute paths from the repo-root confinement; the write sink at `:793` (`AtomicWriteFile`, `write_file`) and `:676` (`edit_file`) run with **no** `guardSymlinkWithinRepo`. The asymmetry is the bug: `read_file` (`:940`) and `get_symbol_source` **do** call `guardSymlinkWithinRepo`; the write path does not.

### PoC (executed)

findings.title: DOMShell: domshell_eval classified as read-tier can execute side-effecting JavaScript without --allow-write
findings.summary:
### Summary

The `domshell_eval` MCP tool (and the `eval` command inside `domshell_execute`) was classified as **read-tier**, allowing it to run without the `--allow-write` server flag. However, `eval` and the write-tier `js` command dispatch to the same handler in the extension and call CDP `Runtime.evaluate` with the raw expression string and no side-effect gate. Any JavaScript expression could therefore mutate DOM, window, or global state through `domshell_eval` without the operator's `--allow-write` authorization.

The tool description explicitly promised "(read-only) ... always available in read-only mode" — the misclassification contradicted the documented contract, not just an implicit one.

### Impact

No new capability was exposed — the same write access was already available via `domshell_js` with `--allow-write` — but the tier misclassification meant:

- MCP hosts (Claude Desktop, Cursor, etc.) rendered the wrong approval UI (`readOnlyHint: true`)
- Server-side tier flags (`--allow-write`) misrepresented what an AI agent was actually authorized to do
- Audit logs and deny messages labeled write-tier activity as read-tier
- Downstream tools and analysis relying on the tier separation could over-trust an `eval` call

Framing: OWASP LLM Top 10 LLM06 (Excessive Agency), NIST AI RMF (tool permission boundary + human-approval fidelity), CWE-863 (Incorrect Authorization).

The reporter's main framing: **the MCP approval UI and server-side permission model can misrepresent the actual agency being granted to an AI agent.**

### Affected code paths

- `mcp-server/index.ts:113` — `WRITE_COMMANDS` excluded `eval`

- `src/background/index.ts:3282` — `handleJs` calls `cdp.evaluateJs(code)`

findings.title: Mareforma: Unsigned Claims Can Be Promoted to REPLICATED via Missing Signature Enforcement in Convergence Path
findings.summary:
### Summary

`mareforma` 0.3.3 contains a critical integrity flaw in the REPLICATED convergence logic (`_maybe_update_replicated_unlocked()` in `mareforma/db/core.py:1300-1319`). The peer-selection SQL query that determines whether two independent claims "agree" on the same anchor does not verify that either claim carries a valid cryptographic signature from an enrolled validator key. Because `rekor_enabled=False` is the default and automatically sets `transparency_logged=1` at insert time, every claim — signed or not — immediately satisfies the convergence precondition. An attacker with no Mareforma key can write an unsigned claim to a shared graph, cause it to converge with a legitimate signed peer claim, and have it promoted to `REPLICATED` status. The forged `REPLICATED` row is then returned by the default trust query (`graph.query(min_support="REPLICATED")`), allowing the attacker to inject false trust signals into any downstream consumer relying on `REPLICATED` as a multi-party endorsement guarantee.

### Details

**Root cause — `mareforma/db/core.py:1300-1319`**

The convergence function `_maybe_update_replicated_unlocked()` selects peer claims using a SQL query that filters on `status`, `unresolved`, `transparency_logged`, and `artifact_hash`, but contains no predicate on `signature_bundle` or enrolled-key identity:

```python

rows = conn.execute(
    f"""
    SELECT DISTINCT c.claim_id, c.generated_by
    FROM claims c, json_each(c.supports_json) j
    WHERE j.value IN ({placeholders})
      AND c.claim_id != ?
      AND c.generated_by != ?
      AND c.support_level != 'ESTABLISHED'
      AND c.status = 'open'
      AND c.unresolved = 0
      AND c.transparency_logged = 1
      AND (
          c.artifact_hash IS NULL
          OR ? IS NULL
          OR c.artifact_hash = ?
      )
    """,
```

findings.title: NATS Server: MQTT SUBSCRIBE Protocol Injection via Leaf Node/Route Forwarding allows arbitrary NATS command injection
findings.summary:
### Background

NATS.io is a high performance open source pub-sub distributed communication technology, built for the cloud, on-premise, IoT and edge computing.

The NATS Server supports MQTT clients and can bridge MQTT activity into NATS subjects across routes and leafnode connections.

### Problem Description

An MQTT client could include protocol control characters in subscription filters that were later forwarded as NATS protocol data to route or leafnode connections.

This could corrupt the forwarded protocol stream and allow injection of unintended NATS protocol operations, potentially across cluster nodes or accounts where route or gateway connections are present.

Anonymous MQTT deployments are higher risk because no credentials are required to reach the affected parser. Authenticated deployments are still affected for clients allowed to create MQTT subscriptions.

### Affected Versions

Versions v2.14.0, v2.12.8 and below are vulnerable. The issue is fixed in v2.14.1 and v2.12.9.

### Workarounds

Disable anonymous MQTT access where it is not required. Deployments that need MQTT have no known complete workaround other than upgrading.

### References

 * GHSA advisory: <https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server/security/advisories/GHSA-qrcv-3558-gj4f>
 * Credit: @thesecguy45

findings.title: PGPainless: Unbounded Compressed Packet Descent in inline-detach and MessageInspector leads to Denial of Service (DoS)
findings.summary:
### Summary
An architectural security boundary bypass in inline-detach and MessageInspector allows remote, unauthenticated attackers to force unbounded recursive decompression routines. By supplying a specially crafted OpenPGP message containing deeply nested compressed packet structures, an attacker can completely bypass the library's built-in DoS protections (MAX_LAYER_DEPTH = 16), leading to resource exhaustion, thread blocking, and potential Out-of-Memory (OOM) application crashes.

### Details
The pg-painless core processing pipeline implements a defensive threshold constraint to prevent decompression bomb sequences (Zip Bombs) and arbitrary resource consumption:

    Enforcement Location: pgpainless-main/pgpainless-core/src/main/kotlin/org/pgpainless/decryption_verification/MessageMetadata.kt

    Threshold Constant: MAX_LAYER_DEPTH = 16

However, a code architecture review revealed two specific packet-walking implementations that unpack and step through PGPCompressedData packets manually, entirely failing to track or increment a layer depth index counter against the static compliance limits:

    In InlineDetachImpl.kt (Line ~78-93): The logic loops over data packets via compressedData.dataStream. Because it processes the incoming data block-by-block without leveraging or passing constraints down to the guarded OpenPgpMessageInputStream tracking mechanism, it accepts infinite nesting.

    In MessageInspector.kt (Line ~95): The inspector utility descends recursively down nested compressed packet layouts to ascertain inner content classification markers (e.g., determining encryption states) without referencing or respecting maximum layer depth boundaries.

findings.title: Miren Runtime: Authentication bypass in RPC layer: unverified TLS client certificates grant cluster superuser access
findings.summary:
### Summary

  The Miren Runtime RPC server (QUIC/HTTP3, default port `:8443`) requested TLS
  client certificates but never verified that a presented certificate chained to
  the cluster Certificate Authority. Because a client-certificate identity is
  granted a blanket RBAC bypass, any party able to reach the RPC listener could
  present a forged, self-signed certificate and be authenticated as a cluster
  **superuser** — no valid CA signature, credential, or prior authorization
  required.

### Impact

  This is a complete, unauthenticated authentication bypass against the cluster
  control plane. An attacker who can reach the RPC port can perform any RPC
  operation with full privileges: enumerate and manipulate entities, apps,
  sandboxes, disks, and other cluster resources. This yields full compromise of
  confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the cluster and everything it
  orchestrates.

  Exposure is network-reachability–gated only. Deployments that expose `:8443`
  beyond a trusted network (e.g. `0.0.0.0/0`) are remotely exploitable from the
  internet by anyone; deployments that restrict `:8443` to a trusted network are
  exploitable by any party with access to that network.

Due to a lack of ability to detect if the RPC has been accessed unauthorized,
Miren recommends that all applications are redeployed and any credentials reference
in environment variables are rotated. A read-only script to help review standing access,
recent changes, and the exact secrets to rotate is available at https://github.com/mirendev/runtime/tree/089582a132f7fc1e1d5b5c0aee1e0911535fed53/scripts/security/audit-exposure.


### Details

  Three independent factors combined to produce the bypass:

  1. **The listener never verified the client-certificate chain.** When a cluster
     CA was configured, the RPC listener used `tls.RequestClientCert`, which
     requests a client certificate but does not verify it against the configured
     `ClientCAs`. `tls.ConnectionState
